title: StreeTalk
text:
Place Pulse 2.0
A significant source of street perception data is the “Place Pulse” project. It collects public feedback on various urban areas using a pairwise labeling interface. Initiated in 2010, the project’s website showcases roughly 4,000 images from four cities: Boston, New York, Linz, and Salzburg. As shown in Figure 1, it gauges public perception across six dimensions. Participants are presented with pairs of street views and asked, “Which image looks safer?”
Over the years, the dataset was enhanced to version 2.0, which includes 110,998 random street-view images gathered from 56 cities in 28 countries across six continents. From 2013 to 2016, 81,630 online participants took part in the survey, providing over 1,170,000 pairwise comparisons. Its geographic and participant coverage made it a useful large-scale benchmark for studying perceived qualities of urban scenes, while still requiring care when transferring models across local contexts.



The Place Pulse interface collects pairwise judgments about street scenes.

title: Sidewalk Ballet at Venice
text:
NoteResearch context



MIT City Form Lab and Hasso Plattner Institute collaboration My role: Sidewalk Ballet project lead at MIT. This page documents the collaborative research and its public installation at the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale. The group-detection methods connect with MINGLE and my doctoral dissertation, now titled Sidewalk Ballet.



The collaboration
Sidewalk Ballet examines where social activities occur on city sidewalks and public spaces. The project uses computer vision and vision-language models to identify situations in which people talk, eat, walk together, play, or otherwise participate in a shared activity. These observations can then be mapped across a city and compared with pedestrian movement and the spatial context of each street.
The project is a collaboration between the MIT City Form Lab and the Artificial Intelligence and Intelligent Systems group at the Hasso Plattner Institute. Andres Sevtsuk directs the City Form Lab. At MIT, I lead the Sidewalk Ballet project, with Freya Huying Tan contributing to the project team. Marco Cipriano leads the work at Hasso Plattner Institute with Gerard de Melo as co-principal investigator.


My role
As the MIT project lead, I have worked on the research pipeline for detecting social interactions in street imagery, coordinated the project’s development at MIT, and led the translation of the work into a public installation. Some methods used in this collaboration also appear in my independent doctoral research, including MINGLE, but the dissertation and the lab project remain distinct in scope and authorship.



The Sidewalk Ballet collaboration translates street-level social-interaction analysis into a public installation.




Venice Architecture Biennale 2025
The City Form Lab exhibit at the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale presented Sidewalk Ballet alongside NYC Walks. The installation was configured as a working graduate-student desk, showing the tools, visualizations, and research process behind city-scale analyses of pedestrian movement and social interaction.
The exhibit formed part of The Next Earth: Computation, Crisis, Cosmology, the MIT Department of Architecture exhibition at Palazzo Diedo. It ran from May 10 to November 23, 2025.

title: Road Asset Assessment in Ulaanbaatar
text:
NoteProject context



CitoryTech commission for the Ulaanbaatar municipal government · World Bank-supported infrastructure program My role: Project lead at CitoryTech, responsible for the analytical approach, system development, and delivery. The work led to a 2022 article in Computational Urban Science.



The decision problem
Ulaanbaatar needed a repeatable way to inspect road and sidewalk infrastructure across the city. Municipal vehicles already traveled through the street network and collected imagery. The project converted those images into a condition-monitoring system that could help staff decide where field inspection and selective repair were most urgent.
The system evaluated nine types of road and transportation assets, including pavement damage, sidewalks, curbs, road markings, signs, manholes, and guardrails. Each detected asset was assigned a condition category and linked to its road segment. Maintenance priority could then consider both physical condition and the importance of the location, including how many people were likely to use it.


My role and delivery
The World Bank introduced our team to the municipal client. I led the project through method design, model development, system integration, and delivery. The final product was a monitoring platform with an interactive map, color-coded road segments, and image-level evidence for the assessed assets.
This format allowed staff to move from a citywide overview to individual locations rather than relying on a single aggregate score. The analytical output was designed to support maintenance prioritization, reporting, and targeted field verification.



The monitoring platform links road-segment condition indicators to the underlying street imagery.




Method and limitations
The workflow combined asset detection with condition assessment. Labeled images supplied the training data, while geo-referenced predictions connected each observation to the road network and the monitoring interface.
The model’s coverage was limited to the asset categories represented in the training data. Adding a new asset type, or encountering a substantially different image source, required new labels and model evaluation. We treated the platform as an updateable inspection aid rather than a replacement for municipal judgment or field checks.


Publication

Zhang, D., Yi, H., Chen, Y., Jiang, N., Shao, J., & Liu, L. (2022). “An Urban Infrastructure Assessment System Built on Geo-Tagged Images and Machine Learning.” Computational Urban Science, 2(1), 1–21. Paper

title: Qiuhao
text:
NoteProject context



CitoryTech product development · Documented version: October 2021 My role: Founder and director, leading the product team. Qiuhao brought recurring planning and consulting workflows into three connected modules: visual indicators, collaborative image collection, and image-based perception surveys.



  
    Qiuhao brings together tools for collecting urban imagery, learning how people perceive places, and mapping image-based indicators of environmental quality. It grew from recurring needs in our planning and consulting projects.
  


From individual projects to a shared workflow
Our clients asked different questions about the urban environment: which streets felt comfortable to walk along, where neighborhood conditions needed attention, or how to assess road infrastructure and storefront design. These projects repeatedly required the same underlying work: gathering images, organizing human assessments, running computer vision models, and connecting the results to geographic locations.
Qiuhao organized this work into three connected modules. Its Chinese name, 秋毫, refers to noticing fine details. The product’s focus was to make visible features of urban space available for systematic assessment and planning decisions.

  
    Module A
    Visual indicator platform
    Analyze imagery and compare places through maps and indicators.
  
  
    Module B
    Collaborative image collection
    Collect field photographs and connect them to online analysis.
  
  
    Module C
    Image-based perception surveys
    Gather visual preferences and use them to support assessment models.
  



Visual indicator platform
The platform organizes image-derived spatial data into a workspace for exploring environmental conditions. Users can browse indicators, select a study area on a map, and compare patterns across locations. The interface connects maps with summary statistics and image examples, so users can examine the observations behind an indicator.



The visual indicator platform presents environmental measures alongside maps, distributions, and image examples. Original interface from the 2021 product materials.


Low-code tools support the construction of analysis workflows. Other views support geographic selection and the visualization of spatial variation. These functions were designed to help planning teams work with image-based evidence through a common interface.

  
    
    Low-code workflow: connect processing steps through a visual interface.
  
  
    
    Spatial selection: define an area and inspect its image-derived indicators.
  

The product design envisaged a standard SaaS service and private deployments with customized modules. The business plan presented the Ulaanbaatar road-condition assessment platform as an example of a project-specific deployment.


Collaborative image collection
The collection module connects fieldwork with image analysis. CityEye, a WeChat mini application, lets participants contribute photographs to a shared survey project, browse a common image collection, and locate observations on a map. It provides a practical way for a group to document a site together.



CityEye links a mobile field-survey tool to a shared desktop image workspace. The original Chinese interface is retained.


An algorithm platform connects the collected imagery to recognition services, image management, map visualization, and data downloads. Customized collection workflows also supported panoramic cameras and vehicle-mounted cameras. The Tianjin Xincun neighborhood assessment shows how a walking survey with a 360° camera could bring narrow residential lanes into this type of assessment.


Image-based perception surveys
Visible objects alone do not describe how people experience a place. The survey module gathers judgments about images, including preferences concerning the appearance of buildings, streets, and neighborhoods.
In a pairwise survey, a participant sees two images and selects the one that better matches a stated criterion. Repeated comparisons provide preference data that can inform image ratings and the development of automated assessment models. The prototype connected study selection, image comparison, and results reporting in a mobile interface.

  
    
    Choose a study. Browse surveys about different places and visual qualities.
  
  
    
    Compare two images. Answer a focused question about their visual qualities.
  
  
    
    Review the results. Inspect rating distributions and image groups. Values shown are part of the original prototype.
  

Customized surveys could use different participant groups, interface designs, and annotation methods, including marking regions within images. The StreeTalk project illustrates the earlier use of visual preferences to model perceived street safety and inform pedestrian routing.


Use in planning practice
Qiuhao’s modules could work together or support a specific stage of a project. A neighborhood study might combine field photography with residents’ visual judgments and a map of local conditions. An infrastructure study could instead emphasize object recognition and a customized inspection interface.
The intended users included planning and design teams, urban management organizations, researchers, and commercial property teams. The common task was to turn images and assessments into spatial evidence that people could inspect and compare. Perception scores describe visual judgments; their interpretation depends on the survey question, participating population, and imagery used.

title: MINGLE
text:
NoteResearch context



Method developed within my MIT dissertation, Sidewalk Ballet My role: Lead author, working with collaborators at MIT and the Hasso Plattner Institute. MINGLE was published at AAAI 2026, in the AI for Social Impact Track. It also supports the City Form Lab collaboration exhibited at Venice.
People can usually recognize who is interacting with whom in a street scene, but a social group has no fixed visual boundary. MINGLE (Multi-person Interaction-aware Neural Group Localization and Extraction) combines person detection, depth-aware vision-language reasoning, and spatial aggregation to locate these groups. The paper also introduces annotations and metadata for 100,000 urban street images.

title: MINGLE
text:
Stage 1: Person detection
An ATSS-Swin-L-DyHead detector first identifies all individual people in the scene with high-confidence bounding boxes. This separates the problem of finding people from the problem of reasoning about their relationships.

title: MINGLE
text:
Stage 2: Pairwise affiliation classification
For every pair of detected individuals, MINGLE constructs a prompt containing:

RGB crops of each person’s bounding box
A depth-map crop of the scene, generated by a monocular depth estimator
Numeric depth values and absolute depth differences inserted directly into the text prompt

This multimodal prompt is fed to a fine-tuned Qwen2-VL / Qwen2.5-VL model, which classifies each pair as interacting, not interacting, or uncertain. Depth cues help distinguish image-plane proximity from estimated physical separation, which is important when perspective places unrelated people close together in an image.
Computational cost is managed by filtering out pairs whose image-plane distance or depth difference exceeds configurable thresholds, reducing the number of VLM calls with limited loss of accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: MINGLE
text:
Stage 3: Group aggregation
A greedy clustering algorithm merges pairwise classifications into group regions. A set of two or more individuals with mutual “interacting” links forms a social group, and a bounding box is computed from the extreme coordinates of its members. The resulting social group region represents collective structure rather than a single body.



MINGLE detects individuals, classifies pairwise affiliation with depth-aware prompts, and aggregates the results into group regions.


Figure 3. The full MINGLE pipeline (top row) and its output format (bottom row). Stage 1 detects individuals; Stage 2 classifies each person pair using depth-aware VLM prompts; Stage 3 aggregates pairs into group bounding boxes. The bottom row shows how group detections and a Social Activity Index are computed for a given street image.

title: National Mobility Networks in China
text:
NoteResearch context



Research collaboration with Hongmou Zhang My role: Lead analyst responsible for geospatial analysis, network analysis, and visualization. Working with Hongmou Zhang, Pensen Wang, and Jinhua Zhao, we examined regional structure using Tencent mobility data. The research began in 2015 and led to a peer-reviewed article published in 2026.



Research question
Administrative boundaries provide one view of a region, but daily mobility often connects places across those lines. This project examined whether large-scale movement networks could reveal regional structures that are clustered, overlapping, or spatially discontinuous.
The analysis used anonymized location-based social-network traces aggregated to 2,242 county-level units. It compared population distribution and movement matrices across workdays, weekends, National Day, and the Spring Festival period.



County-level population and mobility patterns used to compare regional structure.




Analytical approach
County-level units were represented as nodes and movement between them as weighted links. Community detection identified groups of places with strong internal connections without requiring every member to share a border. Network layouts provided a second view in which geographic distance was removed and strongly connected places moved closer together.
This combination made it possible to compare three forms of regional structure:

spatially continuous clusters that resemble familiar metropolitan regions;
cross-boundary connections that extend beyond established planning regions; and
enclaves or breaks produced by strong mobility links between non-adjacent places.




Network views connect places by mobility rather than by geographic proximity alone.




Findings
The resulting communities overlap with several established urban regions, including the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei, Yangtze River Delta, Pearl River Delta, and Chengdu-Chongqing systems. They also reveal discontinuities and long-distance ties that conventional contiguous regionalization can obscure.
Provincial boundaries remain visible in many communities, suggesting that administrative organization still shapes mobility. Other clusters extend across those borders, showing why functional regions are better treated as graded and networked rather than as fixed lines.



Regional communities identified from mobility links, including cross-boundary and discontinuous connections.




Publication and earlier dissemination

Zhang, H., Liu, L., Wang, P., & Zhao, J. (2026). “Reconceptualizing Regional Boundaries: Depicting Blurred Regions in China through Individual Mobility Data.” Computational Urban Science, 6(1), 5. Paper

Earlier versions of the work were presented at the 2016 China Urban Planning Annual Conference and discussed in two Chinese-language essays: City Clusters and City Flows.

title: How Green Are the Streets?
text:
NoteResearch context



Research collaboration with Ying Long My role: Coauthor. The study developed and compared image-based street-greenery measures across Chinese city centers. Published in PLOS ONE in 2017. Read the paper.



Measuring visible greenery
How much greenery is visible from the street? We analyzed over one million Tencent Street View images from central areas of 245 Chinese cities, using color analysis to estimate a green view index and aggregate it across streets and blocks.



Measurement workflow, from directional images to street and block indicators.




Comparing cities
Seasonal imagery differences led us to restrict the comparative analysis to 131 cities. The maps distinguish average greenness from its variation within each city, revealing differences that a single citywide score can hide.



City comparisons: average green view index and within-city variation.




Reading the measure carefully
Color-based greenery estimates can include non-vegetation objects and vary with season and lighting. They describe the sampled views, rather than total vegetation coverage or measured health outcomes.

title: Recognizing Central Activity Zones
text:
NoteResearch context



Research during my planning practice at the China Academy of Urban Planning and Design I developed this study with Zhuqing Liu during my CAUPD period, before CitoryTech. It uses Shanghai POI data from August 2016; the related Springer book chapter was published in 2018.



Planning question
How can a city identify a central activity zone where several urban functions overlap? This study examined both the intensity and diversity of activities in Shanghai, using evaluated points of interest to compare potential boundaries rather than relying on a single concentration of offices or shops.



Overview of the proposed central activity zones in Shanghai.




Dataset
The analysis assembled 386,628 POI records within Shanghai’s outer ring, updated to August 2016. Sources included Dianping and Anjuke. Records were organized into six categories: retail, catering, office, recreation, leisure, and culture. Available attributes, including ratings and prices, supported the evaluation of individual places.



POI distribution and categories used in the Shanghai analysis.




Method
The method combines two dimensions of functional mixture:

Intensity: normalize and aggregate category-specific value maps to locate concentrations of activity.
Diversity: overlay the category maps to identify places where several functions intersect, using entropy to characterize functional mixture.




Aggregated functional values across Shanghai, with the core area enlarged.





Functional intersections across Shanghai, with details for Lujiazui, Nanjing Road, and Zhongshan Park.





Combined functional values, mixture contours, and the fourteen leading mixed-use areas within the middle ring.




Comparing candidate zones
Combining intensity and diversity identified areas with substantial activity across multiple functions. The analysis highlighted fourteen mixed-use areas within the middle ring and used them to explore alternative definitions of the central activity zone. The maps characterize the POI mix; they do not directly measure pedestrian activity or social life.



Selected areas with high functional intensity and diversity.





Three scenarios for defining Shanghai’s central activity zone boundary.

title: Liu Liu
text:
I am a Ph.D. candidate in Urban Science at MIT, advised by Professor Andres Sevtsuk. Working across urban studies and computational social science, I develop and critically evaluate AI methods for understanding human behavior and social life in cities. My central question is how emerging computational methods can produce credible and actionable knowledge about urban life.
My dissertation, Sidewalk Ballet, connects street-level imagery, observations of human activities and interactions in public space, and GIS analysis to study sidewalk life across cities. MINGLE, my method for detecting socially interacting groups, laid part of its methodological foundation. I also investigate the reliability of computational evidence: Clarity or Confusion examines what computer vision measures contribute to urban research, while Sidewalk Moments tests whether richer visual and multimodal representations better reflect human judgments.
I spent three summers as an Applied Scientist Intern at Amazon, working on multimodal learning and reasoning evaluation at AGI and cross-modal video retrieval at AWS. As a visiting researcher at UCLA, I contributed to the 2D semantic component of WalkOCC, a sidewalk-robot perception project. Before returning to MIT, I founded CitoryTech, an urban analytics company, and led its research and consulting work for nearly six years. Our projects served municipal and private-sector clients, spanning spatial analysis, pedestrian environments, and infrastructure assessment. These included road and sidewalk asset assessment in Ulaanbaatar under a World Bank-supported infrastructure program.
At MIT’s City Form Lab, I contribute to pedestrian-flow research and lead the MIT side of Sidewalk Ballet, a collaboration exhibited at the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale. My publications span urban research and AI venues, including Nature Cities, Cities, AAAI, and ECCV. I have also supported courses in urban design, GIS, spatial analysis, and comparative land use and transportation at MIT.

title: Child- and Age-Friendly Streets
text:
NoteProject context



Street-environment research and assessment at CitoryTech · Shanghai · 2021 My role: Project lead at CitoryTech.



The question
How can a city identify street environments that better support children and older adults? I led this project at CitoryTech to connect the everyday requirements of these groups with observable street conditions and access to neighborhood services.
The work combined street imagery, computer vision, points of interest, and spatial analysis. It organized the evidence into four dimensions—safety-related conditions, health-related conditions, convenience, and comfort—so that an overall assessment could be traced back to specific features of a street.



Street-level indicator maps from the project. The four panels show the framework’s safety, health, convenience, and comfort dimensions; they represent environmental assessments rather than observed health or safety outcomes.




From street observations to indicators
The framework brought together features such as sidewalk continuity and condition, crossings, curb ramps, separation from motor traffic, greenery, street furniture, and access to services. Image-derived observations and geographic measures were organized into a hierarchy of indicators.
The documented workflow divided the street network into 50-metre segments and used nearby imagery to identify segments with visual coverage. Spatial measures were standardized against the Shanghai study area and combined through weighted aggregation. Keeping the indicator hierarchy visible allowed a reader to examine the components behind a composite score.







Dimension
Examples of the conditions examined




Safety-related conditions
Walking continuity, crossings, separation from traffic, and accessibility features


Health-related conditions
Green visibility, walking and cycling space, seating, and public-space cleanliness


Convenience
Access to commercial, educational, medical, recreational, and public-transport facilities


Comfort
Street enclosure, greenery, visual character, and environmental attractiveness






The assessment interface presents the indicator hierarchy, connecting the four main dimensions to more specific street and service measures.




My role and project output
I led the CitoryTech team’s work on the project. The materials brought together an indicator framework, spatial calculations, street-level maps, and a web assessment interface. Together, these outputs made it possible to move between an overall view of neighborhood conditions and the individual measures that informed it.



The project’s web interface introduces the assessment of street environments for children and older adults.




Interpreting the assessment
The indicators describe features of the built environment. Image-based perception scores are model-estimated judgments, and the resulting maps do not by themselves establish whether a street produces better health outcomes or is experienced as safe by every child or older adult. The framework provides evidence to examine alongside field observations and the experiences of residents.

title: C-IMAGE
text:
NoteResearch context



MIT master’s thesis and related research I developed C-IMAGE to study the city as represented in geotagged photographs, working with Bolei Zhou on image analysis. The work led to papers in GeoJournal and at ECCV.



Research question
What can photographs reveal about the places people choose to record? Building on Kevin Lynch’s study of the image of the city, C-IMAGE used scene recognition to map recurring features in user-contributed photographs across 26 cities. These maps describe the photographed city: they reflect contributors’ choices and platform coverage, rather than a representative survey of residents’ perceptions.



C-IMAGE compares the spatial distribution of scenes represented in geotagged photographs.




Data and processing
Photographs and geographic coordinates were collected through the Panoramio and Flickr APIs. The broader collection reached approximately 30 million images. Coordinates linked image classifications to locations, allowing visual patterns to be compared within and across cities.



Workflow for collecting and processing geotagged photographs.




Scene classification
The project used Places scene-recognition models to classify image content into 102 attributes. Classes relevant to public space were then organized into seven broader visual categories for mapping. This translated a large image collection into a smaller set of interpretable spatial layers.



Scene categories used to describe the content of the photo collection.




Mapping the photographed city
Mapping these categories reveals where different parts of a city’s public image are concentrated. For example, comparing greenery-related photographs in Shanghai and Tokyo provides a way to examine differences in the places represented in each collection. Such comparisons need to account for uneven photography and platform use.



Spatial patterns in the seven visual categories across selected cities.




More detailed categories
The same workflow can support finer classifications. In a subsequent application, the greenery category was divided into seven subcategories to distinguish different forms of green-space imagery.



A more detailed classification of greenery-related scenes.




Interactive maps
The original interactive maps have been recovered from my archive:
Amsterdam, Bangkok, Barcelona, Beijing, Hong Kong, Kuala Lumpur, London, New Delhi, New York, Paris, Prague, San Francisco, Seoul, Shanghai, Singapore, Tokyo, Toronto, Vienna, Zurich.

title: Clarity or Confusion
text:
NoteResearch context



Independent research at MIT with my advisor, Andres Sevtsuk This review examined what computer vision measures in urban studies and planning. Published in Cities in 2024, it analyzes 146 papers and 104 street attributes, with a closer assessment of 24 quantitative studies. Its gaps in the measurement of human activities and interactions shaped my dissertation, Sidewalk Ballet.



Research question
The paper asks three related questions: What specific data can computer vision collect that interests planners and urban designers? How have planning researchers actually used these data? And what fundamentally new knowledge has computer vision contributed to planning?
Traditional observation — the tradition of Whyte, Gehl, Lynch, and Jacobs — is rich but labor-intensive and hard to repeat across a city. Computer vision promises to extend the counting and mapping of street environments with far less effort. Whether that promise has translated into clear, well-defined measures is the question the title poses.


Review scope
A three-stage screening of the Web of Science identified 146 influential papers, from which we extracted and classified 104 distinct street attributes into four groups:

Visual Dominants — large scene components such as greenery, sky, buildings, and roadways, mostly measured as pixel ratios from semantic segmentation.
Micro-Level Details — discrete elements such as street furniture, signs, wires, and pavement condition, typically from object detection.
Composite Metrics — indices assembled from multiple attributes, such as walkability, bikeability, and perception scores.
Deep Features — learned representations without direct physical definitions, used in perception and scene-comparison studies.




The three data models behind CV street attributes: image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection, each producing a different data type for urban analysis.


The three data models behind CV street attributes: image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection, each producing a different data type for urban analysis.
The review then traces how these attributes flow into research topics — walkability, housing prices, health, climate, safety — across the quantitative studies that use them.



How research topics (left) draw on CV-derived street attributes (right) across the reviewed literature. A small set of attributes, led by greenery, serves most topics.


How research topics (left) draw on CV-derived street attributes (right) across the reviewed literature. A small set of attributes, led by greenery, serves most topics.


Findings
Beyond the catalog itself, the review identifies three structural problems in the field:

Ambiguity of definitions. Many attributes lack clear, consistent definitions; the same term can denote different measurements across papers.
Unbalanced research focus. Effort concentrates on model and feature selection, while measurement validity and standardization receive far less attention.
Unclear effectiveness. In the 24-paper subcollection, how much explanatory power street attributes add to urban models is often difficult to establish.

Across the review, many different urban questions depend on a small family of readily extractable metrics, especially greenery. This creates a mismatch between what urbanists want to understand and what computer vision is equipped to measure. Human activities and interactions — central to classic observational studies of public life — remain weakly represented.
The review calls for clearer definitions and standardized measurement. It also shaped the starting point for Sidewalk Ballet, my dissertation: begin with an urban question, define the observable evidence it requires, and then develop the method to measure it.

title: Population and Urban Growth
text:
NoteProject context



Commissioned research for Jinmao Group · CitoryTech · 2020 My role: Project lead at CitoryTech.
Watch the population and urban growth visualization.



The question
Where were people concentrating, where was urban land expanding, and how closely did these changes align? I led this consulting project at CitoryTech to compare the development trajectories of five major Chinese city regions: Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei, the Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta, Chengdu–Chongqing, and the middle reaches of the Yangtze River.
The study connected a national view of population distribution with comparisons among cities, their urban cores, and surrounding areas. It gave the client a common analytical framework for examining regional differences in urban growth.



Population distribution in Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei, shown in the project’s map interface. The regional views connected dense urban cores with their wider settlement patterns.




Data and approach
Our team combined LandScan population grids with DMSP/VIIRS night-time light data. The report examined population change over 2000–2018 and light-derived built-up-area change over 1992–2016. Regional maps, population cartograms, growth comparisons, and spatial hot-spot analysis offered complementary views of the same urban systems.







Analytical step
What it revealed




Population distribution and change
Concentrations of people and areas of growth or decline


Comparisons within city regions
Differences between core cities and surrounding places


Built-up-area trajectories
The timing and extent of urban land expansion


Population–land comparison
Places where population and land growth followed different paths






Population-growth hot spots and cold spots across the five study regions. Warm and cool colors identify spatial clusters in the historical estimates.




Comparing growth trajectories
The analysis identified distinct patterns: population concentration with relatively limited land expansion, land expansion outpacing population growth, and more balanced growth at lower rates. These comparisons made it possible to examine variation within a city region alongside differences between regions.



Population growth plotted against built-up-area growth, with cities grouped by region. The comparison highlights different relationships between demographic change and physical expansion.




My role and project output
I led the CitoryTech team’s work on this project. The output was a comparative research report supported by maps and visual analysis, bringing population change, urban expansion, and regional structure into one discussion for the client.
The figures document the historical study delivered in 2020. Population grids and night-time lights are estimates of spatial conditions; their comparison describes patterns of change rather than establishing that land development caused population growth.

title: NYC Walks
text:
NoteResearch context



MIT City Form Lab collaboration My role: Collaborator in geospatial data engineering, spatial computation, model validation, and research visualization. The work was published in Nature Cities and exhibited alongside Sidewalk Ballet at Venice.



Project overview
Walking is central to urban travel, but cities rarely have consistent pedestrian counts for an entire street network. NYC Walks developed a citywide model of foot traffic during six peak travel periods in New York City. The model estimates pedestrian volumes across a network of 315,577 connected sidewalk, crosswalk, and footpath segments.
The work uses urban network analysis to connect trip origins and destinations through the pedestrian network, then calibrates the resulting estimates against observed counts. The citywide model provides a common baseline for comparing pedestrian demand, street classifications, infrastructure needs, and exposure to traffic risk.


My contribution
Within the broader City Form Lab team, I:

contributed to large-scale geospatial data engineering and spatial computation;
tested and validated workflows used to detect and assemble sidewalk and crosswalk networks;
produced pedestrian-flow figures and visual comparisons between estimated volumes and observed counts; and
contributed analyses and revisions to the published paper.

Andres Sevtsuk conceived the research design. Modeling, calibration, safety analysis, and writing were shared across the author team.


Findings and planning applications
The published analysis identifies outer-borough streets whose estimated foot traffic is comparable with parts of central Manhattan but whose official classifications give them less pedestrian priority. It also compares crash counts with estimated pedestrian exposure and finds that some of the highest exposure-adjusted risks occur outside Manhattan.
These results show how a citywide pedestrian baseline can help agencies identify places where infrastructure classification, investment, and observed demand do not align.



City-scale pedestrian network analysis in New York City.




Publication

Sevtsuk, A., Basu, R., Liu, L., Alhassan, A., & Kollar, J. (2026). “Spatial Distribution of Foot Traffic in New York City and Applications for Urban Planning.” Nature Cities, 3, 136–145. Paper

title: Sidewalk Ballet
text:
NoteResearch context



MIT doctoral dissertation in Urban Science · Expected completion: June 2027 Committee: Andres Sevtsuk (chair), Jinhua Zhao, and Lawrence Vale.
Sidewalk Ballet connects a measurement framework, studies of sidewalk social life, and a national data resource. The related papers are:

Method: A Vision-Language Framework for Measuring Social Life on Sidewalks, with Andres Sevtsuk — under review at Computers, Environment and Urban Systems; preprint available.
Data: Stay Together: Street-Level Social Indicators for Sidewalk Life Across 496 U.S. Cities, with Andres Sevtsuk — manuscript in preparation.
Methodological foundation: MINGLE — published at AAAI 2026. The dissertation extends this group-detection work to activities and spatial measures; the findings study is ongoing.
This project measures how people use sidewalks: who is moving or staying, who is together, and what they are doing. My MIT dissertation uses street-level images and vision-language models to extend close observation of public life across streets and cities. It asks what pedestrian counts miss when equally busy sidewalks support different activities and forms of social presence. The measures describe what is visible at the moment an image was captured.

title: Sidewalk Ballet
text:
Recognize social groups
A social group is a relationship among people, so proximity alone is insufficient. Occlusion, depth differences, and the lack of motion in a still image make it difficult to distinguish people together from people who happen to be close. The framework detects people with SAM3, estimates depth with PatchFusion, and uses a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-3B model to judge pairs before assembling them into groups. The preprint reports F1 = 80.64% for this pairwise model, using an expanded 76K training corpus.

title: Sidewalk Ballet
text:
Describe visible states
Alongside grouping, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct records ten fields per person: validity, posture, locomotion, object, object relation, support surface, zone type, uniform presence, apparent age group, and model-perceived sex. Separating these fields lets a person be recorded as walking, holding a phone, and occupying a particular part of the sidewalk, rather than forcing the observation into a single activity label. The preprint reports 88.5% mean field accuracy on 999 held-out samples.
The vocabulary draws on Whyte and Mehta’s observational research. It distinguishes visible states from interpretations of intent or social meaning. Apparent age and model-perceived sex are exploratory estimates; sex is excluded from primary analyses because provider face blurring makes it unreliable.



Examples from the attribute vocabulary: posture, locomotion, objects and object relations, support surfaces, spatial zones, uniforms, and apparent age. Labels describe model readings of visible evidence; apparent age is an exploratory estimate.

title: Sidewalk Ballet
text:
Connect groups and activities
The two branches inform one another. A validity filter removes detections in advertisements, inside vehicles, or outside the target pedestrian space before groups are rebuilt. Group-level consistency helps refine locomotion labels; group IDs then join to the per-person fields. Rules applied to these records produce activity, spatial-context, and accessibility-related indicators, with location and capture time retained for every observation.

title: Sidewalk Ballet
text:
Build interpretable measures
Grouping and dwelling summarize two aspects of the scenes shown above. Each person receives a grouping weight \(\alpha\): 1 when alone, 2 in a pair, and 3 in a group of three or more. A dwelling weight \(\beta\) is 3 for a stationary, seated person who is not riding; 2 for a stationary, non-seated person; and 1 otherwise.









Index
Definition
What it summarizes




Weighted Grouping Index (WGI)
\(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\alpha_{g(i)}\)
Grouping composition


Weighted Dwelling Index (WDI)
\(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\beta_{s(i)}\)
Observable dwelling posture


Social Dwelling Index (SDI)
\(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\alpha_{g(i)}\beta_{s(i)}\)
Grouping and dwelling combined for each person




SDI averages the per-person products of the two weights, which is why scenes with similar headcounts can differ. These ordinal measures describe visible configurations, rather than the duration of a visit, someone’s reasons for being there, or the quality of a social experience. The method paper reports sensitivity checks for alternative weights.

title: Sidewalk Ballet
text:
Keep capture time explicit
Imagery with capture timestamps is organized into four observation windows: weekday and weekend, each at 12:00–14:00 and 17:00–19:00. This keeps the observed activity tied to when it occurred. The broader collection includes Apple Look Around, Bing Streetside, and Mapillary; the national analysis below uses the Apple and Bing subset.

title: Sidewalk Ballet
text:
From panorama to sidewalk-facing views
Each panorama is reprojected into left and right sidewalk-facing views, with a 150° field of view and a 1600 × 800 pixel frame. The original presentation figure links the two photographs to the capture point, road direction, and opposite viewing directions on the street network, preserving which side of the street each image observes.

  

From street view to side view: the red arrows connect the two photographs to their sidewalk-facing directions on the road network. Click to view the full presentation figure.

title: Sidewalk Ballet
text:
Keep intersections distinct
At intersections, a wide view retains corners and crossings together. These records remain separate from mid-block views. For spatial analysis, sidewalk-facing observations are assigned to side-specific block frontages on the TIGER/Line road network, while intersection records retain their junction association. View and frontage identifiers, capture time, and a road-segment crosswalk support linkage to land use, transportation, and demographic data.

  

An intersection panorama and the corresponding collection of intersection locations on the street network. Click to view the full presentation figure.

title: Sidewalk Ballet
text:
Compare like with like
The national analysis examines grouping (WGI) and visible posture and locomotion (WDI) separately. SDI is included in the planned release but not used in this paper’s empirical analysis. Comparisons must also account for crowd size: a view containing one person necessarily has WGI = 1, so pooling different person counts can reverse an apparent association with neighborhood density.
Holding the detected count at exactly two people, the share classified as one group falls from 38.0% in the lowest tract-density quintile to 26.8% in the highest. This descriptive pattern demonstrates the importance of the comparison being made; it does not establish that density causes less socializing.



Grouping and tract density, conditioning on the number of detected people and capture window. The pooled relationship differs from the within-count patterns.

title: Sidewalk Ballet
section: Build a research resource with explicit limits
text:
Build a research resource with explicit limits
The national maps summarize grouping and dwelling where the imagery supports measurement. People were detected on 430,984 frontages (11.6%); grouping and dwelling are undefined on the rest. The median frontage has one view. Coverage is opportunistic, and the national sample has not received an independent annotation audit, so these records support research on observed configurations rather than validated rankings of places.



National patterns in grouping and dwelling across 6,066 measurable 2-km grid cells in 472 cities, with grouping shown within twelve selected cities. The full dataset covers 496 cities.


The panel is assembled and in use. Derived tables, schemas, and documentation are being prepared for public release; source imagery will not be redistributed.

title: Sidewalk Moments
text:
NoteResearch context



Independent research on urban visual experience My role: Study lead, with Freya Huying Tan and Fábio Duarte. The manuscript is being prepared for submission, with a preprint available. This strand complements my research on the measurement of public life by testing how different representations relate to human judgments.



Research question
Video retains motion and temporal order, so it is often treated as a richer representation than a still image. Richer, however, does not necessarily mean closer to human judgment. Sidewalk Moments asks which visual representations best preserve the moments that viewers find engaging while moving through a city.


Study design
The study uses 61 first-person city-walk videos from YouTube, segmented into more than 50,000 ten-second clips. Each clip is represented in four ways:

spatiotemporal video features;
temporally averaged images;
audio embeddings; and
text-based semantic descriptions.

The analysis first compares these representations with a continuous engagement signal derived from viewer replay behavior. It then tests their ability to classify high- and low-engagement moments. An independent two-alternative forced-choice experiment provides a separate comparison with human judgments.



Study framework linking four representations to engagement prediction, human validation, and analysis of cases in which video and temporally averaged images diverge.


Study framework linking four representations to engagement prediction, human validation, and analysis of cases in which video and temporally averaged images diverge.


Main finding
Video features align most strongly with the continuous engagement signal, following the expected ordering by temporal richness. That ordering changes in binary classification. Temporally averaged images match or outperform video across most tested classifiers and thresholds, and participants in the human study identify engaging moments with comparable accuracy from temporally averaged images and full clips.
The gap analysis suggests that the two representations retain different information. Video performs better in activity-driven scenes with dynamic content, while temporally averaged images align more closely with judgments in scenes dominated by stable spatial composition.
These results make representation a substantive choice in urban research: it determines which aspects of a scene a model retains and which it leaves out. Richer features cannot simply be assumed to be better proxies for human experience. Here, replay behavior provides a specific signal of engagement, complemented by human validation; it does not stand in for every aspect of perception or experience in public space.


Paper and presentation

Liu, L., Tan, F. H., & Duarte, F. (2026). “Sidewalk Moments: Are Richer Representations Always More Human-Aligned? Evidence from City-Walk Videos.” Preparing for submission. arXiv

Publication entry. The work was presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the American Association of Geographers in San Francisco. Presentation materials

title: TOD Station-Area Assessment
text:
NoteProject context



World Bank study · Beijing · CitoryTech project, 2019 · Published January 2020 My role: CitoryTech project lead and second author of the World Bank report.


A metro station can be well connected to the transit network while offering an uncomfortable or inconvenient walk outside its entrances. This project asked how planners could assess those environments consistently across a city. I led CitoryTech’s analysis team and coauthored the resulting World Bank working paper with Wanli Fang and Jianhao Zhou.

  
    
  
  
    World Bank Working Paper · January 2020
    Assessing Physical Environment of TOD Communities around Metro Stations
    Using Big Data and Machine Learning
    Fang, W., Liu, L., & Zhou, J. (2020). World Bank, Washington, DC.
    World Bank publicationRead PDFDOI
  


Define the pedestrian catchment
The study covered 201 metro stations within Beijing’s Fifth Ring Road, measuring conditions within each station’s 10-minute walking catchment. Rather than applying a fixed-radius buffer, these areas followed the street network, accounting for disconnected streets, major roads, and other barriers.
The resulting walking catchments ranged from 53 to 208 hectares. That variation is itself useful planning evidence: stations with similar geographic proximity can provide very different access to surrounding neighborhoods.



Ten-minute walking catchments at Muxidi, Huagong, Yongdingmenwai, and Huoqiying stations. Their shapes reveal constraints imposed by road networks and barriers. World Bank report, Figure 10, p. 12; basemaps: Gaode (AMap).




Combine access and street experience
Street-view imagery supplied evidence about what pedestrians encounter outside the station. We combined image recognition, models of human visual perception, and spatial analysis with points of interest and transit information. The framework organized this evidence into four dimensions and 14 indicator groups.







Dimension
Evidence examined




Convenience
Transit connections, walking and cycling access, amenities, and mixed urban functions


Comfort
Sky openness, visible greenery, lighting, seating, and predicted perceptions of safety and aesthetics


Vibrancy
Image-based observations of pedestrians, bicycles, vehicles, and street vendors


Characteristics
Similarity and uniqueness of station-area streetscapes






The published framework links four assessment dimensions to 14 indicator groups. The report’s safety and aesthetics indicators represent predicted visual perceptions. World Bank report, Figure 4, p. 7.




Compare stations in context
For citywide comparison, the report normalized indicators to a common scale and used the Analytic Hierarchy Process to aggregate convenience, comfort, and vibrancy. Streetscape clustering identified six types of station-area landscapes, including historic, commercial-office, high-rise, suburban, park, and green urban settings. Aggregation weights varied by landscape type, recognizing that station areas have different contexts.



Station-area landscape categories across Beijing and relationships among visually similar station areas. World Bank report, p. 38.




Turn profiles into local priorities
Station profiles connected the comparative assessment back to specific streets. At Guomao, the report identified strong transit connections, abundant amenities, and high vibrancy, alongside more moderate comfort and limited streetscape distinctiveness. Its proposed improvements included more diverse vegetation, compatible cultural or artistic elements, and a more bicycle-friendly environment.



Guomao station’s indicator profile and street-view examples connect transport access, urban functions, and street conditions. World Bank report, p. 38.


The aim was to support targeted station-area improvements and a repeatable basis for comparison across stations, corridors, and future surveys. The report presents diagnostic findings and possible interventions; it does not evaluate the effects of implemented changes.


My contribution and scope
I led the CitoryTech team’s work and am the report’s second author. The acknowledgements identify me as Data Scientist (consultant) and credit the street-view and big-data analysis to Liu Liu, Jinxin Shao, Hongdu Yi, Ding Zhang, Nan Jiang, and Xin Xiong at CitoryTech. The World Bank study was conducted under the GEF Sustainable Cities Integrated Approach Pilot Project (P156507).
The measures describe conditions visible in the sampled imagery. Predicted safety is a visual judgment; people and vehicles detected in an image are observations rather than measured traffic flows. The published assessment focuses on environments outside metro stations, with station interiors discussed as future work.
Related work: CityEye, CitoryTech’s collaborative image-collection tool, and the Nanjing Livable Neighborhood Assessment, a separate field-survey and image-analysis project.
Figures are cropped from Fang, Liu, and Zhou (2020), © World Bank, under CC BY 3.0 IGO. The walking-catchment basemaps are credited in the report to Gaode (AMap). Original figure colors, labels, and plotted values are retained. Publication and full report.

title: WalkOCC
text:
NoteResearch context



Collaborative research at UCLA’s Vision and Autonomy Intelligence Lab My role: Collaborator on the 2D semantic component. The broader team developed the hybrid 2D–3D occupancy framework. A preprint is available, with a revised manuscript in preparation.



Project overview
WalkOCC studies monocular 3D semantic occupancy perception for robots moving through sidewalks and crossings. The full project combines limited paired LiDAR and RGB sequences with a larger collection of 2D-only images. A ray-marching consistency objective connects 2D semantic supervision with 3D occupancy learning.
The resulting framework addresses a practical constraint in sidewalk robotics: paired 3D sensor data and occupancy annotations are expensive, while monocular street imagery is much easier to collect at scale.



Overview of the hybrid 2D and 3D learning framework. Figure from the WalkOCC project page.


Overview of the hybrid 2D and 3D learning framework. Figure from the WalkOCC project page.


My contribution
My work focused on the 2D semantic component. I:

fine-tuned SAM 3 on sidewalk-robot imagery to segment fine-grained elements including curbs, gutters, crosswalks, and driveways;
participated in discussions of the semantic taxonomy and evaluation design;
audited annotations and identified inconsistencies, including rider versus motorcycle segmentation and ambiguous driveway versus sidewalk boundaries; and
supported the hybrid study’s 2D semantic component and coauthored the manuscript.

These tasks draw on my urban visual research, particularly the definition and validation of street-level categories, while extending it toward environments shared by pedestrians and autonomous machines.
